newsitem.title: USA: Treasuries need +150,000 US payrolls to keep rally.
newsitem.headline: Treasuries need +150,000 US payrolls to keep rally.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries are poised to continue their week-long rally, but the market needs help from Friday's October employment data, experts said on Thursday.
Nonfarm payrolls are expected to have risen by 212,000 in the month, according to a Reuters survey, with forecasts ranging from up 150,000 to 300,000.
"To really put more juice into the rally, it'll have to be 150,000 or lower," said Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
But the market is looking at more than payrolls.
Market participants said average hourly earnings, aggregate hours worked and the unemployment rate will all be important in determining how the market reacts.
"What moves most gets the most attention," said Matthew Alexy, chief market strategist at CS First Boston Corp.

Analysts agreed that for the market to break below recent ranges, payrolls need to be low, the unemployment rate needs to be above 5.3 percent and average hourly earnings cannot rise more than 0.4 percent.

Alexy said that if those major components point to weakness, the long bond can break below 6.58 percent and perhaps as low as 6.50 percent. In afternoon dealings on Thursday, the bond was yielding 6.69 percent.

Still, most experts aren't predicting another two-point spike up like on Tuesday, when a bond-friendly Employment Cost Index sent the long bond soaring. Analysts said Tuesday's move encompassed the hope of another bullish jobs report.

On the other hand, players said, payrolls well above the consensus, coupled with an unemployment rate of about 5.0 percent, and earnings above 0.5 percent, would likely send bond prices down one point and yields back up above 6.75 or 6.80 percent.
"But there won't be a (bond market) meltdown," said Terry Piggot, head trader at Daiwa Securities America Inc.
However, market participants were split on what might happen if the report is neutral.
"If we get a consensus number, I am not sure what that means," said Piggot. "Do we average the two months?"
Payrolls fell a surprising 40,000 in September, and the market expects a big rebound from that quirky number.

Some experts foresee a minimal response, since it was built in. Others forecast a small bounce if the numbers come in at or near consensus, which would suggest the market reveling in the continued moderate economic growth/low inflation phase.
But Platt said anything but a weak number would push Treasury yields higher, since the next hurdle will be supply. He pointed out that the market tends to cheapen yields up ahead of auctions.
The Treasury next week will sell $18.5 billion three-year notes, and $10 billion each of 10-year notes and 30-year bonds in its quarterly refunding effort.
"Generally, average-to-better news sees us doing better," Piggot of Daiwa said. "But the market would love an excuse to go down to get supply cheaper."
